https://auto.economictimes.indiatimes.co.text: The concerns gained attention after Norwegian public transport company Ruter tested two buses last year and found potential security risks linked to OTA technology.Auto makers are increasingly using over-the-air (OTA) software updates, a technology that smartphone companies like Google, Apple and Samsung have relied on for more than a decade to deliver new features and security fixes. While the technology has made updating vehicles faster and cheaper, cybersecurity experts are warning that it also creates new risks. According to a CNBC report, analysts say wireless updates could leave connected vehicles vulnerable to cyberattacks, data breaches and even attempts by foreign actors to interfere with vehicle systems.OTA updates raise cybersecurity concerns: AnalystOver-the-air (OTA) technology allows manufacturers to wirelessly send software updates, bug fixes and new features to internet-connected devices without requiring a visit to a service center.Tesla began rolling out OTA updates for its Model S vehicles in 2012, helping popularize the technology across the automotive industry. Today, many car makers use OTA updates to improve vehicle software and fix issues remotely."The technology is increasingly welcomed as it is a quick and cost-effective way to manage systems on vehicles, over traditional methods which may have required a recall or update at routine maintenance," Siraj Ahmed Shaikh, professor in systems security at Swansea University in the UK, told CNBC.However, analysts say the growing use of OTA updates also introduces new cybersecurity risks.Its use represents "a unique national security concern," Gabriel Lim, senior analyst at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, told CNBC."Aside from data privacy concerns, the potential of a foreign actor sabotaging the controls of a moving vehicle is a possibility that countries like Norway, Denmark, and Britain have expressed concerns about," Lim added.Norwegian bus test highlights potential risksThe concerns gained attention after Norwegian public transport company Ruter tested two buses last year and found potential security risks linked to OTA technology."There is access to the control system for battery and power supply via mobile network through a Romanian SIM card. In theory, therefore, this bus can be stopped or rendered inoperable by the manufacturer," the company said.The findings prompted authorities in the UK and Denmark to launch their own investigations.

https://www.eng.kavkaz-uzel.eu/articles/.text: Homepage / All news 18:58, 18 August 2026 Sources reported the death of the great-grandson of Batal-Khadji Belkhoroev. The great-grandson of the founder of the Batalkhadzhintsy brotherhood, Ilyas Belkharoev, died in Poland, and his relatives are preparing to bury him in Ingushetia. In Russia, Belkharoev was charged with a number of terrorist offenses. As reported by " Caucasian Knot ", Ilyas Belkharoev was among the individuals that law enforcement declared wanted and arrested in absentia in connection with the murder on November 2, 2019, in Moscow, of the head of the Ingush CPB, Ibrahim Eldzharkiev, and his brother Ahmed Eldzharkiev. The murder of Eldzharkiev was recognized as a terrorist act. Batal-Khadji Belkhoroev is an Ingush sheikh, the founder of one of the Qadirite branches (vird), a follower of Sheikh Kunta-Khadji, as reported in a reference published on "Caucasian Knot" titled " Batal-Khadji and his followers ". In 2022, members of the Ingush brotherhood of Batal-Khadji agreed to form several units to participate in battles in Ukraine in response to support from Ramzan Kadyrov for their cause . After arrests, searches, and criminal cases against the Batalkhadzhintsy, Ramzan Kadyrov provided them with public protection. Kadyrov stated that the term "Batalkhadzhin terrorist society" is absurd, and the Belkharoevs will always be his close friends, but in February 2023, the FSB included the combat wing of the Batalkhadzhintsy in the list of terrorist organizations. 39-year-old Ilyas Belkharoev died in a pre-trial detention center in Poland, and his relatives have already retrieved his body to bury him in his homeland, reported today by “Kommersant” citing several sources. According to the publication, “mourning events are expected to take place on August 19 in the village of Surkhakhi.” Ingush journalists also confirmed the information that the body of Ilyas Belkharoev has already been handed over to his relatives. According to some reports, Belkharoev ended up in a Polish prison due to suspicions of involvement in arms smuggling from Ukraine, while others suggest it was due to a domestic conflict. The exact cause of his death has not been disclosed. “He developed severe chronic depression a long time ago. Ilyas was in a difficult mental state,” one of his sources told “Fortanga.” Belkharoev, who was accused of arms smuggling by Russian law enforcement back in the early 2000s, had been living in Ukraine since 2014. According to law enforcement, he also organized arms supplies to the Russian Federation there: it is believed that it was with Belkharoev's involvement that a Glock pistol ended up in Russia, from which Ibrahim and Ahmed Eldzharkiev were shot in November 2019. In connection with the murder of the Eldzharkievs, Ilyas Belkharoev was charged with terrorism (Article 205 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation). Later, he was additionally charged with participation in a terrorist community and in an illegal armed formation (Articles 205.4 and 208 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation) - as claimed by the FSB, he participated in hostilities against Russian military forces as part of a Ukrainian armed unit commanded by Adam Osmayev. At the same time, Interpol excluded Ilyas Belkharoev from its wanted database in 2022, recognizing his persecution as politically motivated. Russian law enforcement attributes the nickname ingbanderovec to Belkharoev. One of Ilyas Belkharoev's brothers insists that he did not participate in hostilities. Photograph: Reuters Saudi Arabia Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport after air-raid alerts in Saudi capital Authorities also issued warnings for Jeddah and Yanbu, a major industrial port and home to vital oil facilities Donna Ferguson and agencies Sat 19 Sep 2026 10.54 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 10.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday after the government sent air-raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks. Explosions were heard in the capital and firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport. It is the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen escalated in July. Residents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital. According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there are “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index. “In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity. The Saudi civil defence force sent air-raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities. Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflict Read more The all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds. The UN security council condemned the continued ​Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children. It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen, where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes , the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group. The Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group also says the Saudi air force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days. The Houthis recently seized control of strategic the Red Sea islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis. Manage Preferences Amendments to the Occupational Health and Safety Act that take effect on October 26 will give employers the right to test employees for intoxication. However, according to the Labor Inspectorate, this does not mean that every workday can now begin with a breathalyzer test. Under the new rules, employers may test employees for intoxication if there are reasonable grounds for suspicion. For example, suspicions may arise if an employee behaves unusually, slurs their speech or displays other signs of possible intoxication. An exception applies to workplaces where working while intoxicated could have particularly serious consequences. If an employee's duties involve operating potentially hazardous equipment or they work in an environment involving such hazards, the employer may conduct intoxication tests even without reasonable suspicion. This could apply, for example, to bus and truck drivers, operators of dangerous machinery and construction workers. The aim of the amendment is to prevent workplace accidents and protect employees, their colleagues and others. Employers cannot conduct intoxication tests at their own discretion. Before conducting tests, they must establish written procedures and inform all employees of them. These procedures must clearly specify how testing will be conducted, what constitutes a positive result, the potential consequences of such a result and what happens if an employee refuses to be tested. Employees' rights must also be protected and they must have the opportunity to challenge test results. Employers may retain intoxication test data for up to three years from the date of testing. The Labor Inspectorate emphasizes that the purpose of intoxication testing must be to ensure workplace safety, not to subject employees to unjustified checks.
